practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes a Wide Area Network (WAN)?
A) A network covering a small area such as a school building, owned by one organisation
B) A network that uses Bluetooth to connect personal devices over a short range
C) A network covering a large geographic area that relies on third-party telecommunications infrastructure
D) A network that connects two computers in the same room using a cable
practice_questions.marks: C) A network covering a large geographic area that relies on third-party telecommunications infrastructure [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State one characteristic of a wired network that makes it more suitable than a wireless network for a school’s computer lab.
practice_questions.marks: Any one of: higher speed / more reliable / more secure / less susceptible to interference [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term IP address.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A numerical label assigned to every device on a network, used to uniquely identify and locate it so that data packets can be correctly routed to their destination.
Secure: A unique identifier for a device on a network used for routing.
Developing: A number that identifies a device on the internet.
Emerging: A device address (too vague). [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe two ways in which a wireless network connection differs from a wired network connection.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Any two contrasts, each clearly explained: (1) Wireless transmits data using radio waves whereas wired uses physical cables — meaning wireless devices can move freely but wired devices are fixed. (2) Wireless connections are generally slower and more susceptible to interference from walls and competing signals, whereas wired connections are faster and more reliable. (3) Wireless signals can be picked up by any device in range, making unauthorised access easier than with a wired connection. (4) Wireless range is limited by distance from the access point.
Secure: Two contrasts identified with reasonable detail.
Developing: Two differences stated without development.
Emerging: One difference stated. [2 marks per difference]

practice_questions.text: A software developer needs to upload a 400 MiB project file to a remote server. The upload speed of their internet connection is 80 Mbit/s. Calculate how long the upload will take. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Step 1 — File size in bytes: 400 × 1024 × 1024 = 419,430,400 bytes. Step 2 — Convert to bits: 419,430,400 × 8 = 3,355,443,200 bits. Step 3 — Divide by rate: 3,355,443,200 ÷ 80,000,000 = 41.94 seconds (approximately 42 seconds). Award method marks for correct approach even if arithmetic error.
Secure: Correct method shown; minor arithmetic error at most.
Developing: Correctly converts bytes to bits OR correctly divides but not both.
Emerging: Sets up the division but uses incorrect units throughout. [3 marks: 1 mark per correct step]

practice_questions.text: Explain the role of routers in making the internet work.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A router reads the destination IP address on each incoming data packet and forwards it along the best available path towards that destination. Routers connect multiple networks together and make routing decisions independently at each hop. Because there is no single central router, if one route is unavailable the traffic can be redirected along an alternative path — making the internet resilient.
Secure: Correctly explains packet forwarding and path selection; mentions IP addresses.
Developing: States routers direct traffic but does not explain how (IP addressing or path selection).
Emerging: Describes a router as connecting the internet without explaining its function. [4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'decomposition' in the context of problem solving.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Breaking a complex problem (1) into smaller, more manageable sub-problems, each accomplishing an identifiable task (1). Both parts needed for 2 marks.
Secure: Correct idea with one component missing or vague.
Developing: Vague — e.g. 'splitting a problem up' without reference to sub-problems or identifiable tasks.
Emerging: Confuses decomposition with abstraction.

practice_questions.text: A developer is building a school library management system. Identify two sub-problems that could be created by decomposing this problem.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Any two valid sub-problems, each clearly identifiable and distinct, e.g. searching for a book, recording a loan, sending overdue reminders, managing member accounts, reserving books. 1 mark for each valid sub-problem, up to 2 marks.
Secure: One valid sub-problem.
Developing: Vague — e.g. 'looking up books'.
Emerging: Describes a feature rather than a sub-problem.

practice_questions.text: Explain what is meant by abstraction and describe what is abstracted away when a sat-nav calculates a route.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Abstraction defined as removing unnecessary detail (1), keeping only information relevant to solving the problem (1). In a sat-nav, detail removed includes road surface conditions, lane width, tree locations, precise building positions (1). Only relevant data is retained: distances, speed limits, road connections (1).
Secure: Correct definition with a valid example but explanation of what is removed is partial.
Developing: Example given but definition missing or incorrect.
Emerging: Confuses abstraction with decomposition.

practice_questions.text: Describe two benefits of structuring a program using subprograms.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct benefits, each described with a supporting detail: e.g. reusability — written once, called from multiple places, reducing repeated code (2); testing in isolation — each subprogram tested independently with known inputs before integration (2). 2 marks per benefit.
Secure: Two benefits named but supporting detail thin for one.
Developing: One benefit described fully; second vague or missing.
Emerging: Benefit named without any description.

practice_questions.text: A team of five developers is building a social media platform. Explain how decomposition would help them work on the project simultaneously.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Decomposition breaks the platform into sub-problems (1), each assignable to a different developer (1), so all five can work in parallel (1), reducing overall development time (1).
Secure: Parallel working explained with two marks' worth of detail.
Developing: Decomposition mentioned but link to parallel working vague.
Emerging: Generic or off-topic.

practice_questions.text: Discuss the benefits and drawbacks of using subprograms when developing a large banking application. Consider reusability, testing, complexity and any trade-offs.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: At least three benefits identified and explained (reusability — same validation logic called across multiple screens; testing in isolation — each payment subprogram tested separately; reduced complexity — code is easier to read and maintain) (3 marks). At least one trade-off identified and explained (designing clear interfaces between subprograms requires upfront planning; poorly named subprograms can be confusing) (2 marks). Balanced conclusion (1 mark). 6 marks total.
Secure: Two benefits and one trade-off with some reasoning. 4–5 marks.
Developing: Two benefits listed with little explanation; no trade-off. 2–3 marks.
Emerging: One point with no reasoning. 1 mark.

practice_questions.text: State the most appropriate data type for storing a student's date of birth in the format DD/MM/YYYY.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: String (1). The format contains slashes and leading zeros — it cannot be stored as an integer or real without losing information.
Secure: Correct with minor explanation gap.
Developing: Character (a single symbol only — cannot hold the full date).
Emerging: Integer or Boolean.

practice_questions.text: Define what is meant by a constant in a Python program. Give one reason why a programmer would use a constant rather than a variable.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A constant is a named value (1) that is set once and should not change during execution (1); reason — if the value needs updating, it is changed in one place rather than in every occurrence in the code (1); example given, e.g. TAX_RATE or MAX_LIVES (1).
Secure: Constant correctly defined with a weak reason.
Developing: One part (definition or reason) correct.
Emerging: Confuses constant with variable.

practice_questions.text:
A Python program contains the line:
score = input("Enter score: ")
total = score + 10
Explain why this will cause an error, and write a corrected version of the second line.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: The input() function returns a string (1) so adding 10 (an integer) to a string is a type error (1); corrected line: total = int(score) + 10 (1); explanation that int() converts the string to an integer (1).
Secure: Error correctly identified with partial correction.
Developing: Identifies an error exists but misnames the type.
Emerging: No understanding of type conversion.

practice_questions.text: Identify the data type of each of the following Python values: (a) True  (b) 3.14  (c) 'K'  (d) 42
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: (a) Boolean (1), (b) real/float (1), (c) char (1), (d) integer (1).
Secure: Three correct.
Developing: Two correct.
Emerging: One or none correct.

practice_questions.text:
Complete a trace table for the following Python code. Show the value of total after each iteration.
total = 0
for i in range(1, 4):
    total = total + i
print(total)
practice_questions.marks:

practice_questions.text:
A programmer writes the following code:
MAX_SIZE = 100
studentnumber = 0
Write a brief explanation of why MAX_SIZE follows good programming practice, and suggest an improvement to the identifier name for the second variable.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: MAX_SIZE is in uppercase — conventional for constants (1); its name clearly describes its purpose (1); it can be changed in one place if the limit changes (1); studentnumber could be improved to student_number or studentNumber (1); a better name describes the purpose more precisely, e.g. currentStudentNumber or studentCount (1); explanation of why the improvement matters for readability and maintenance (1).
Secure: Three or four valid points with partial explanation.
Developing: One or two points without full reasoning.
Emerging: Vague or no understanding of naming conventions.

practice_questions.text: Describe the role of the control unit in the fetch-decode-execute cycle.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: The control unit manages and coordinates the entire fetch-decode-execute cycle. It sends signals to RAM via the control bus to indicate whether the operation is a read or write. During the decode stage, it interprets the instruction to determine which components must act and what data they need. It then directs the ALU, registers and memory accordingly during execute.
Secure: States the control unit manages the cycle and decodes instructions, with some reference to directing other components.
Developing: States the control unit manages the CPU or decodes instructions, but lacks supporting detail.
Emerging: Vague reference to the control unit being involved in processing.

practice_questions.text: Explain the purpose of the address bus during the fetch stage of the fetch-decode-execute cycle.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: During fetch, the CPU places the address of the next instruction on the address bus. The address bus carries this address to RAM so RAM knows which memory location to access. The address bus is one-directional (CPU to RAM). This allows the correct instruction to be located and placed on the data bus to travel back to the CPU.
Secure: States that the address bus carries the address of the instruction to RAM, with some explanation of why this is needed.
Developing: States the address bus is used during fetch but does not explain its direction or purpose clearly.
Emerging: Names the address bus without explaining its role.

practice_questions.text: State the three stages of the fetch-decode-execute cycle in the correct order.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for all three correct and in order: fetch, decode, execute.

practice_questions.text: Name the component of the CPU that performs arithmetic and logical operations.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: ALU (accept: arithmetic logic unit).

practice_questions.text: Describe what happens during the decode stage of the fetch-decode-execute cycle.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks for: the control unit (1 mark) examines or interprets the instruction to determine what operation is needed and which components must act / what data is required (1 mark). Accept references to the control unit identifying the operation type. No bus activity is required during decode.

practice_questions.text: Discuss whether increasing clock speed is always the best way to improve CPU performance. Consider the role of the clock and other factors that affect performance.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A higher clock speed means more pulses per second, so the CPU can start more fetch-decode-execute cycles each second and work through instructions faster. However, a faster clock alone has limits: it generates more heat and can make the processor unstable. The CPU also has to fetch every instruction and every data item from RAM along the buses, and RAM is much slower than the CPU, so the processor can end up waiting for data however fast the clock runs. Concludes that clock speed is only one factor, and that how quickly instructions and data reach the CPU from main memory matters as well.
Secure: Explains that a faster clock means more cycles per second, gives at least one limitation (heat, instability, or waiting for RAM), and reaches a judgement.
Developing: Explains that a faster clock means more operations per second and mentions one limitation without development.
Emerging: States that clock speed affects performance, with little or no development.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is the correct denary value for the 8-bit two's complement pattern 10001010?
A) 138
B) -118
C) -10
D) -128
State the hexadecimal value that is equivalent to the 8-bit binary pattern 11110000.

Correct method shown — subtracting place values in order [1 mark]
Correct result: 01001001 [1 mark]

practice_questions.marks:
Step 1: Write +13 in binary: 00001101 [1 mark]
Step 2: Invert all bits: 11110010 [1 mark]
Step 3: Add 1: 11110011 [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Convert the hexadecimal value B7 to binary. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
B = 1011 [1 mark]
7 = 0111 [1 mark]
Full answer: 10110111 [full marks only if both nibbles correct]

practice_questions.text: Explain why hexadecimal notation is used when working with binary data. Include an example to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: States that hex is a compact shorthand for binary (1), each hex digit represents exactly 4 bits / one nibble so conversion is straightforward (1), long binary strings are difficult for humans to read and write accurately (1), appropriate example given (e.g. MAC address, colour code, memory address shown in hex) (1).
Secure: Two or three of the four points present with some development.
Developing: States hex is shorter but no explanation of the nibble relationship.
Emerging: Vague — 'hex is easier' with no development.

practice_questions.text: State the name and year of the UK law that gives individuals the right to request deletion of their personal data held by an organisation.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering/Secure: Data Protection Act 2018. Developing: Data Protection Act (year missing or wrong). Emerging: Any other act named.

practice_questions.text: Describe what is meant by 'planned obsolescence' and explain one environmental consequence it causes.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Planned obsolescence is the practice of designing products to become outdated or to lose software support after a limited period (1), encouraging consumers to replace devices sooner than necessary (1); this increases the volume of e-waste generated (1); discarded devices contain hazardous materials such as lead and mercury that can leach into soil and groundwater if sent to landfill (1). Secure: Correct definition plus one environmental consequence clearly explained. Developing: Planned obsolescence described but consequence vague or not linked to specific harm. Emerging: Term used without explanation.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ethical concerns raised by organisations collecting personal data from users.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Ownership — the platform that collects data may claim ownership even though the data relates to the user's personal behaviour; this raises the question of who has rightful control (1+1). Consent — users may not have meaningfully agreed to their data being used in specific ways; long, complex privacy policies can obscure what is actually being consented to (1+1). Misuse — data collected for one purpose (e.g. fitness tracking) could be shared with insurers or employers and used to make decisions that negatively affect the user (1+1). Award any two concerns fully explained. Secure: Two clear concerns with explanation. Developing: One clear concern explained; second is vague. Emerging: Privacy mentioned without explanation.

practice_questions.text: A software developer writes a new application. Identify the type of intellectual property protection that automatically applies to this software from the moment it is created.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering/Secure: Copyright. Developing: Copyright, Designs and Patents Act (acceptable — identifies the correct law). Emerging: Patent or trademark (incorrect — these require registration).

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'software licence'.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: A legal agreement between the rights holder and a user that sets out the terms under which software may be used, modified or distributed (2). Secure: Mentions legal agreement and permitted use (2). Developing: Partial — describes a licence as 'permission to use software' without mentioning legal/contractual nature (1). Emerging: Vague description with no legal dimension (0).

practice_questions.text: Discuss the view that the benefits of collecting large amounts of personal data outweigh the ethical and legal risks involved.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Benefits — personalised services improve user experience; health monitoring data can improve medical outcomes; analytics can drive business efficiency and economic growth (two developed points). Risks — privacy breaches expose sensitive data; misuse of data by insurers or employers can cause real harm; individuals often lack meaningful consent; organisations may prioritise profit over user welfare; legal obligations (Data Protection Act 2018) can be difficult to enforce globally (two developed points). Evaluation — weighs both sides; reaches a justified position acknowledging trade-offs between social benefit and individual rights. Secure: Both sides addressed with development; evaluation present. Developing: One side well-developed; other side listed without development; evaluation absent or weak. Emerging: One-sided argument with little supporting reasoning.

practice_questions.text: State the difference between a for loop and a while loop in Python.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A for loop is count-controlled and runs a fixed number of times known in advance (1); a while loop is condition-controlled and runs while a condition is True, so the number of iterations is not fixed (1).
Secure: Both loops mentioned but the distinction is imprecise.
Developing: One loop described correctly without comparison.
Emerging: Both described as identical or neither correct.

practice_questions.text: Write Python code for a program that asks the user to enter a number between 1 and 10. The program should keep asking until a valid number is entered, then print the number.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Variable initialised outside loop (1); while loop with correct condition e.g. num < 1 or num > 10 (1); input() with int() conversion inside loop (1); loop repeats correctly until valid input (1); print() after loop exits (1); meaningful identifier name (1).
Secure: Loop structure correct; minor error in condition or conversion.
Developing: Loop present but condition or conversion wrong.
Emerging: No loop — sequential structure only.

Mastering: i=1 count=0 (odd); i=2 count=1 (even); i=3 count=1; i=4 count=2; i=5 count=2; output 2. Mark per correct iteration row (4 marks for correctly identifying the two even numbers and final count).

practice_questions.text: A programmer wants to write a program that reads exam scores for a class of 30 students and counts how many scored above 75. Discuss whether a for loop or a while loop is more appropriate for this task, and write the Python code.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: For loop identified as more appropriate (1); reason — 30 iterations known in advance (1); counter variable initialised to 0 (1); for loop with range(30) or equivalent (1); if score > 75 inside loop increments counter (1); print result after loop (1).

practice_questions.text: State one cause of algorithmic bias in a machine learning system.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering/Secure: Biased training data — the training data reflects historical human prejudice or discrimination (1). Also accept: unrepresentative training data — certain groups are underrepresented, causing the model to perform less accurately for those groups (1). Emerging: 'Bad data' without specifying bias or representation.

practice_questions.text: Explain what is meant by 'accountability' as an ethical issue with artificial intelligence systems.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Accountability refers to the question of who is responsible for decisions made by an AI system (1); many AI systems are 'black boxes' whose reasoning cannot be explained (1); this means individuals cannot find out why a decision affecting them was made (1); and there is no clear human to hold responsible or appeal to (1). Secure: Correct definition with two explained consequences. Developing: Accountability defined vaguely or one point developed. Emerging: General statement about AI making decisions with no explanation of the accountability problem.

practice_questions.text: Explain why legal liability is a problem when an autonomous vehicle is involved in a collision.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Existing legal frameworks assume a human driver is responsible (1); when operating fully autonomously there is no human driver to hold liable (1); responsibility may fall on the vehicle manufacturer, software developer, deployment company or owner (1); it is unclear how to assign fault between these parties when an algorithm made the decision (1). Secure: Correct identification of the human-driver assumption and two possible liable parties. Developing: Notes liability is unclear but doesn't explain why existing frameworks fail. Emerging: States someone should be responsible but doesn't identify the structural problem.

practice_questions.text: Describe two safety risks associated with using AI systems in high-stakes environments.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Unexpected inputs — AI trained on specific data may encounter real-world situations outside its training distribution, leading to unreliable outputs (1+1 for description plus consequence). Adversarial attacks — deliberately crafted inputs can cause confident but entirely wrong outputs, posing risks in systems used for medical imaging or security (1+1 for description plus consequence). Secure: Two distinct risks described with a linked consequence for each. Developing: Two risks named without linking consequences. Emerging: One risk described.

practice_questions.text: A recruitment company uses a machine learning system to shortlist job applicants. Identify one ethical issue this raises and explain the potential harm caused.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Algorithmic bias (1); if the training data reflects historical hiring patterns where certain groups were discriminated against, the model may learn to replicate those patterns (1); this could result in candidates from those groups being systematically rejected not because of their suitability but because of the biases in the training data (1); this perpetuates inequality and causes real harm to individuals who deserve equal consideration (1). Also accept: accountability — if the system rejects a candidate, they may have no way to find out why or challenge the decision (1+1+1+1). Secure: Correct issue named plus mechanism of harm clearly explained. Developing: Issue named but mechanism described vaguely. Emerging: Issue named with no explanation of harm.

practice_questions.text: Discuss the view that the risks of using artificial intelligence in society outweigh the benefits.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Benefits — AI can diagnose diseases with specialist-level accuracy; machine learning detects financial fraud in milliseconds; robots remove workers from dangerous or repetitive tasks; autonomous systems can improve transport safety by removing human error (two developed points). Risks — algorithmic bias can perpetuate discrimination at scale; accountability gaps mean affected individuals cannot challenge decisions; legal liability frameworks are inadequate; safety failures in high-stakes systems can cause physical harm; displacement of jobs has social consequences (two developed points). Secure: Both sides addressed with development; evaluation present but brief. Developing: One side well-developed; other listed; evaluation absent. practice_questions.text: Define the term network protocol.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: An agreed set of rules that govern how data is formatted, addressed, transmitted and received across a network, allowing devices from different manufacturers and operating systems to communicate reliably.
Secure: A set of rules for communication between devices on a network.
Developing: Rules that devices follow when communicating.
Emerging: Something computers use to talk to each other (too vague). [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe the difference between POP3 and IMAP for receiving email.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: POP3 downloads emails from the server to the local device and typically deletes them from the server — they are not accessible on other devices. IMAP keeps emails on the server and synchronises the state across all devices — reading, deleting or organising an email on one device is reflected on all others.
Secure: Key difference (server deletion vs server storage/sync) correctly identified.
Developing: One protocol correctly described; the other vague.
Emerging: Names both without meaningful comparison. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain the role of the Link layer in the TCP/IP model and identify one protocol that operates at this layer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: The Link layer is responsible for the physical transmission of data across a single network link (e.g. a cable or wireless channel). It uses MAC addresses — unique hardware addresses assigned to each NIC — to identify devices on the local network and deliver data to the correct one. One protocol at this layer: Ethernet (for wired connections) or Wi-Fi (for wireless). Correct explanation of MAC addresses at this layer, contrasted with IP addresses at the Internet layer.
Secure: Role correctly described with one protocol identified and brief MAC address explanation.
Developing: Layer role stated without explanation of MAC addresses; protocol identified.
Emerging: Vague description of the layer; protocol missing or incorrect. [4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of using HTTPS instead of HTTP for a school’s online homework portal.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Advantages — HTTPS encrypts data in transit so student login credentials and submitted work cannot be read if intercepted; browser shows a padlock, building trust; protects against man-in-the-middle attacks. Disadvantages — slightly higher processing overhead (encryption and decryption take time and computing resource); requires a valid SSL/TLS certificate which has a cost and must be renewed; may be slightly slower for low-powered devices. Evaluates: for a portal handling sensitive student data, the security benefit of HTTPS outweighs the performance cost, making it the appropriate choice.
Secure: Both sides argued with at least two valid points each; conclusion reached.
Developing: Advantages well argued; disadvantages vague or only one identified.
Emerging: Only advantages or only disadvantages stated; no evaluation. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: State one advantage and one disadvantage of solid-state storage compared to magnetic hard disk storage.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for advantage: no moving parts so faster access / more durable / lighter / uses less power / silent. 1 mark for disadvantage: more expensive per GiB / lower maximum capacity available for the same price.

practice_questions.text: Explain why secondary storage is needed in a computer system.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: RAM is volatile — all data is lost when power is removed, so secondary storage is required to retain files, programs and the operating system permanently. Secondary storage also provides far greater capacity than RAM (multiple TiB vs typically 8–32 GiB of RAM) and can be portable, allowing data to be moved between systems. Mentions that the CPU cannot access secondary storage directly — data must be loaded into RAM first.
Secure: States that secondary storage retains data without power (persistence) and gives one other reason (capacity or portability) with explanation.
Developing: States that secondary storage keeps data when the computer is off, no further development.

practice_questions.text: Define the term embedded system.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks for: a computer system (processor + memory + software) (1 mark) built into a larger device to perform one specific function, which users cannot reprogram (1 mark). Accept examples that illustrate the fixed-purpose nature.

practice_questions.text: A school is setting up a new IT suite. The head of department suggests using HDDs for the computers because they are cheaper than SSDs. Discuss whether HDDs are the most suitable storage for this use case.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: HDDs offer high capacity at lower cost per GiB, which is relevant for a school budget. However, HDDs are mechanical and slower — boot times and file access will be noticeably slower than SSDs, which may affect lesson time and student experience. SSDs are more durable (no moving parts), important in an environment where computers may be knocked. SSDs also use less power. However, if cost is the primary constraint, HDDs may be acceptable if speed is not critical. Conclusion: the decision depends on budget vs performance priorities; a mixed approach (SSD for the boot drive, HDD for bulk storage) could optimise both.
Secure: Identifies cost advantage of HDD and speed advantage of SSD; makes a reasoned recommendation with reference to the school context.
Developing: Contrasts HDD and SSD on one or two features with limited connection to the scenario.
Emerging: Simple statements about HDDs or SSDs without comparison.

practice_questions.text: Give one example of an embedded system and describe what it does.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for a valid example (washing machine controller, engine control unit, smart thermostat, microwave controller, traffic light controller, etc.). 1 mark for describing its function in terms of monitoring input and controlling a specific output or process.

practice_questions.text: Identify which storage type — magnetic, optical or solid-state — would be most suitable for archiving large amounts of data at the lowest cost, and explain why.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Magnetic (HDD) offers the highest capacity at the lowest cost per GiB, making it the most cost-effective choice for archiving large data volumes. The access speed of HDDs is less critical for archival use (data is read infrequently). Mentions that HDDs are more cost-effective than SSDs and have higher capacity per unit than optical media, which would require many discs for large archives.
Secure: Identifies HDD or magnetic storage and gives cost per GiB as the reason; some comparison with at least one other type.
Developing: Identifies a storage type with a relevant reason but no comparison.
Emerging: Names a storage type without explanation.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following describes the effect of a logical right shift by 1 on any 8-bit binary number?
A) Divides the value by 2 and preserves the sign bit
B) Multiplies the value by 2 and fills with 0 on the right
C) Divides the value by 2 and fills the leftmost bit with 0
D) Copies the sign bit into the rightmost vacated position
practice_questions.marks:
C) [1 mark]
A logical right shift fills vacated positions with 0 — it does not preserve the sign bit.

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by overflow in binary arithmetic.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Overflow occurs when the result of an arithmetic operation (1) is too large to be stored in the available number of bits (1).
Secure: Correct idea with one component missing.
Developing: Vague — 'when the number is too big'.
Emerging: Confuses overflow with underflow or a carry bit.

practice_questions.text: Add the two 8-bit binary numbers 01011011 and 00110110. Show your working and state the denary equivalent of the result.
practice_questions.marks:
Working shown with carry row [1 mark]
Correct binary result: 10010001 [1 mark]
Correct denary: 145 [1 mark]
(Check: 91 + 54 = 145)

practice_questions.text:
An 8-bit binary number is 10110100.
(a) Apply a logical right shift of 2 places and write the result. [1 mark]
(b) Apply an arithmetic right shift of 2 places and write the result. [1 mark]
(c) Explain why the two results are different. [2 marks]
practice_questions.marks:
(a) 00101101 [1 mark]
(b) 11101101 [1 mark]
(c) The logical shift fills vacated positions with 0 (1). The arithmetic shift fills vacated positions with a copy of the sign bit, which is 1 for this negative two's complement number, so the sign is preserved (1).

practice_questions.text: A computer uses 8-bit unsigned binary. Explain what happens when 11100000 (224) and 01000001 (65) are added together.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: The true mathematical result is 289 (1), which exceeds the maximum 8-bit value of 255 (1), so overflow occurs (1), the carry bit beyond the eighth bit position is lost and the stored 8-bit result is incorrect / does not represent the intended value (1).
Secure: Identifies overflow and states the result is too large, with two points developed.
Developing: Identifies overflow but explanation is incomplete.
Emerging: Describes the addition without identifying overflow.

practice_questions.text: Discuss the difference between logical and arithmetic binary shifts. In your answer, refer to how each handles vacated bit positions and when each is appropriate.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Logical shift fills all vacated positions with 0 (1), treating the pattern as unsigned (1). Arithmetic right shift fills vacated positions with the sign bit (1), preserving the sign for two's complement values (1). Both left shifts fill with 0 (1). Arithmetic shifts are appropriate for signed (two's complement) arithmetic; logical shifts for unsigned patterns (1).
Secure: Correct description of both types with at least four points.
Developing: One type described fully, the other partially.
Emerging: Describes shifts in general terms without distinguishing the two types.

practice_questions.text: Name two functions of an operating system.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each function correctly named, up to 2 marks: file management / process management / peripheral management / user management.

practice_questions.text: Describe what is meant by process management as a function of an operating system.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks for: the OS controls which programs are running at any time (1 mark) and allocates CPU time between them, switching between processes so they appear to run simultaneously (1 mark). Accept references to pausing waiting processes or scheduling.

practice_questions.text: Explain how a code review helps developers create more robust software.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A code review involves one or more developers reading through code written by a colleague before it is released. The reviewer looks for bugs, logic errors, security weaknesses (e.g. missing input validation, hardcoded credentials) and poor coding practices. Because the reviewer did not write the code, they approach it with fresh eyes and can spot issues the original developer overlooked. Identifying vulnerabilities at design time means they can be fixed before users are exposed to them, making the software safer and more reliable.
Secure: States that code review involves another developer checking the code for errors or vulnerabilities before release, with some explanation of why a second perspective is valuable.
Developing: States that a code review involves checking code for errors, without explaining the mechanism or benefit.
Emerging: Vague reference to checking code.

practice_questions.text: Describe the purpose of an audit trail in a software system.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks for: an audit trail is an automatic log (1 mark) that records who performed each action, what was changed, and when, so that security incidents or unauthorised access can be traced or detected (1 mark).

practice_questions.text: Explain one difference between a code review and an audit trail as methods of making software more robust.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A code review is a design-time technique carried out before the software is released: developers inspect source code to find and fix vulnerabilities before users encounter them. An audit trail is a run-time technique that operates while the software is live: it logs actions automatically so that if something goes wrong (e.g. a data breach), there is a record of what happened and when. The key difference is timing and purpose: code review prevents problems from shipping; audit trails detect and allow investigation of problems after they occur.
Secure: Identifies that one is before release and one operates during use, with some explanation of each.
Developing: Names both techniques and states one difference without development.
Emerging: Names both techniques with no difference stated.

practice_questions.text: Identify which utility program a system administrator would use if files on a magnetic hard disk were taking much longer to open than usual, and explain why this utility would help.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Disk defragmentation. Over time, files on a magnetic HDD become fragmented — their data is split across non-contiguous sectors of the platter. When a file is opened, the read/write head must physically move to each fragment in turn, increasing access time. Defragmentation reorganises the file data so it is stored in contiguous sectors, meaning the head travels less distance and access is faster. Notes that defragmentation applies to HDDs, not SSDs.
Secure: Identifies defragmentation and explains that fragmented files cause the head to move more, slowing access.
Developing: Identifies defragmentation without a full explanation of why fragmentation causes slowness.
Emerging: Names a utility but incorrect or no explanation.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following describes a bus topology?
A) Every device connects to a central switch with its own dedicated cable
B) All devices share a single central cable called the backbone
C) Every device connects directly to every other device
D) Devices are arranged in a ring with data travelling in one direction
practice_questions.marks: B) All devices share a single central cable called the backbone [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Identify the single point of failure in a star topology.
practice_questions.marks: The central switch (or hub). [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe the structure of a mesh topology.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: In a mesh topology, each device connects to multiple other devices, creating redundant paths for data. A full mesh connects every device to every other device; a partial mesh provides multiple paths but not every possible connection. If one link fails, data can travel via an alternative route.
Secure: Multiple connections between devices and the concept of redundant paths identified.
Developing: States devices connect to multiple others but does not mention redundancy or full/partial mesh.
Emerging: Describes a topology with many connections but without accurate structural detail. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why a star topology is more suitable than a bus topology for a school computer lab.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: In a star topology, each computer has its own dedicated cable to the central switch. If one cable is damaged, only that computer loses its connection — the rest of the lab continues to work. In a bus topology, a single break in the backbone cable brings down the entire network. For a school environment where continuous access is important for lessons, the star topology’s fault isolation is a significant advantage. Adding new computers is also straightforward in a star (run a new cable to the switch) without disrupting existing connections.
Secure: Star topology’s fault isolation correctly explained and contrasted with bus backbone failure.
Developing: States star is better and gives a reason but does not explain the mechanism of fault isolation.
Emerging: Names star topology as more suitable without explanation. [4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe two disadvantages of using a mesh topology for a small business network.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Any two of the following, each with detail: (1) Very high cabling and installation cost — a full mesh of n devices requires n(n-1)/2 connections, so adding each new device requires connecting it to every existing device. (2) Complex to configure and manage — each device must handle multiple connections and routing, requiring significant network administration expertise. (3) Uses a large amount of cable or wireless infrastructure, increasing both initial and ongoing costs.
Secure: Two distinct disadvantages identified with some development.
Developing: Two disadvantages stated without sufficient detail.
Emerging: One disadvantage stated. [2 marks each]

practice_questions.text: A company is setting up two networks: one connecting 20 office workstations for everyday tasks, and one connecting three mission-critical database servers that must remain accessible even if a link fails. Discuss which topology is most appropriate for each network.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Office workstations (star): each workstation has its own cable to a central switch. A single cable fault only affects one machine, keeping productivity loss minimal. The switch is the only single point of failure but is easy and inexpensive to replace. Cost is manageable (20 cable runs). Alternative view: mesh would give more resilience but is impractical for 20 office computers due to cost (190 connections needed). Database servers (mesh or partial mesh): three servers with full mesh requires only 3 connections but provides complete redundancy — any server or link can fail without losing access to the other servers. Small number of connections makes full mesh feasible here. Alternative view: star could work with a managed switch if the switch has a redundant power supply, but remains a single point of failure. Conclusion: star is most appropriate for the office (cost-effective, sufficient fault isolation); mesh is most appropriate for the servers (critical resilience requirement, small number of devices).
Secure: Both networks analysed with correct topology recommendation and reasoning; both sides of the argument considered for at least one network.
Developing: Both topologies correctly recommended with some reasoning; limited analysis of trade-offs.
Emerging: One network correctly analysed; the other vague or missing. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'syntax error'.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A syntax error occurs when the rules of a programming language have been broken (1), causing the program to be rejected before it can run (1).
Secure: Correct idea but one part vague (e.g. 'a mistake in the code' without specifying language rules).

practice_questions.text: Identify the type of error in the following situation: a program to calculate a student's average score divides the total by the number of subjects taken. When a student has taken zero subjects, the program crashes.

practice_questions.marks:

Efficiency — count comparisons: finding the largest requires checking every item, so 999 comparisons for 1,000 items (1 mark). Memory — algorithm only needs one variable to store the current largest value, so memory use is minimal (1 mark). practice_questions.text: State the difference between a computer virus and a worm.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: A virus attaches to a host file and requires user action (such as opening an infected attachment) to spread (1); a worm spreads automatically across networks by exploiting vulnerabilities, without needing a host file or user action (1). Secure: Key distinction (host file / automatic spread) clearly made. Developing: One feature of one type stated without comparison. Emerging: Both types mentioned with no meaningful distinction.

practice_questions.text: Explain what ransomware does and describe one measure an organisation could take to reduce the impact of a ransomware attack.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Ransomware encrypts the victim's files, making them inaccessible (1); it then demands a ransom payment, usually in cryptocurrency, in exchange for the decryption key (1). Measure: maintaining regular offline backups means that if files are encrypted by ransomware, they can be restored without paying the ransom (1); backups must be stored separately from the primary system to prevent the ransomware encrypting them too (1). Secure: Correct description of ransomware plus a valid, explained measure. Developing: Ransomware described; measure stated but not explained. Emerging: Ransomware described; measure absent or vague.

practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Phishing uses fraudulent emails or messages that appear to come from a trusted source to trick users into revealing credentials or visiting a fake website (1+1); it is effective because it targets human psychology rather than technical flaws — no vulnerability in software needs to exist for phishing to succeed (1); a user who believes the message is genuine will voluntarily enter their credentials, bypassing password protection entirely (1). Secure: Correct definition and clear reason for effectiveness. Developing: Definition correct; effectiveness described vaguely as 'tricks people'. practice_questions.text: Discuss the view that technical protections such as anti-malware software and encryption are sufficient to protect an organisation's digital systems.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Arguments for sufficiency — anti-malware can detect and quarantine known threats before they execute; encryption makes intercepted data unreadable; together they address the two most common attack vectors (technical intrusion and data theft) (two developed points). Arguments against sufficiency — anti-malware cannot detect entirely new threats (zero-day attacks); encryption does not prevent social engineering where a user is tricked into voluntarily providing credentials; technical protections do not address unpatched software vulnerabilities; human behaviour is not governed by software; acceptable use policies and backup procedures are also necessary to address behaviour and recovery (two developed points). Evaluation — technical protections are necessary but not sufficient; a layered strategy including people, processes and technology is required. Secure: Both sides with development; evaluation present. Developing: One side well-developed; other side listed. Emerging: One-sided with minimal development.

practice_questions.text: Explain how increasing the bit depth of a digital sound recording affects the quality and file size of the recording.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A higher bit depth means more bits per sample (1), so more distinct amplitude levels can be recorded (1), producing more precise volume measurements and higher-quality sound with less quantisation noise (1). More bits per sample increases the total file size because more data is stored per second (1).
Secure: Both effects described (quality improves, file size increases) with some supporting reason.

practice_questions.text: Explain why binary representation of data has limitations when the number of available bits is restricted. Give examples from both images and sound.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Fewer bits mean fewer distinct values can be represented (1). In images, a lower colour depth produces fewer possible colours and visible banding in gradual colour changes (1). In sound, a lower bit depth means fewer amplitude levels, causing audible distortion (quantisation noise) (1). A lower sample rate may also miss rapid changes in the sound wave, losing high-frequency detail (1).
Secure: One medium (image or sound) explained with two correct points.
Developing: Correct general idea (fewer bits = less accuracy) but no specific example developed.

practice_questions.text: Define the term high-level programming language.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks for: a programming language that uses English-like syntax (1 mark) and is portable across different processor types, providing a high level of abstraction from hardware (1 mark).

practice_questions.text: Describe how a compiler translates a high-level language program.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks for: a compiler reads and translates the entire program (1 mark) into machine code in one pass before execution, producing a standalone executable file (1 mark).

practice_questions.text: Explain two differences between a compiler and an interpreter.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Any two of the following, each with justification. (1) Translation timing: a compiler translates the whole program before execution; an interpreter translates one statement at a time during execution. This means compiled code runs faster because no run-time translation is needed. (2) Output: a compiler produces a standalone machine code executable; an interpreter does not — the interpreter must be present every time the program runs. (3) Error reporting: a compiler reports all errors after analysing the whole program; an interpreter stops at the first error encountered, making the error location immediately clear. Each difference must include an explanation of the consequence or reason, not just a bare contrast.
Secure: Two differences stated correctly with some justification for each.
Developing: Two differences stated without justification, or one difference with justification.
Emerging: One difference stated with little or no explanation.

practice_questions.text: Give one advantage of using assembly language rather than machine code.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: assembly language uses readable mnemonics (e.g. MOV, ADD) instead of binary, making it easier to read and write than machine code. Accept any reference to readability, human-readable codes, or the use of mnemonics.

practice_questions.text: Describe one advantage of using a high-level language rather than a low-level language when developing software for a school attendance management system.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: High-level languages use English-like syntax (e.g. Python), making the code much easier to read and understand. In a team environment, other developers can maintain or extend the system without needing to understand the underlying hardware architecture. Additionally, high-level languages are portable — the attendance system could be deployed on different hardware (Windows servers, Linux servers) without rewriting the code. Programmes can also be written and debugged much faster.
Secure: States one advantage clearly (e.g. easier to read, portable) and links it to the scenario.
Developing: States an advantage of high-level languages without linking to the school context.
Emerging: Vague reference to high-level being easier.

practice_questions.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of using an interpreter compared to a compiler for a developer who is writing and testing a new program. In your answer, consider both the development phase and the final product.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: During development, an interpreter is advantageous: it translates and runs one line at a time, stopping immediately at the first error and showing exactly which line failed, giving fast feedback. No compilation step is needed before each test run. However, once the program is finished, interpreted code runs more slowly than compiled code because translation happens at run time. The interpreter must also be installed on every machine that runs the program, adding a dependency. A compiler is slower to use during development (the whole program must be compiled before testing), but produces a standalone executable that runs faster and does not require the compiler to be present. Concludes: interpreters are more convenient during development; compilers produce better final products.
Secure: Identifies interpreter’s advantage for error location during development and compiler’s advantage for speed and standalone execution; some evaluation of trade-offs.
Developing: Describes one advantage of each without evaluating the development vs deployment distinction.
Emerging: Simple statements about one translator with little comparison.

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between penetration testing and ethical hacking.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Penetration testing is a specific technique within the broader discipline of ethical hacking — it involves attempting to access a network or system without legitimate credentials to find vulnerabilities, with written authorisation from the organisation. Ethical hacking is the broader practice that includes penetration testing but also social engineering tests (e.g. attempting to trick staff into giving up passwords), physical security tests (e.g. trying to enter a server room without authorisation), and software code review. Both involve using attacker techniques with permission, distinguishing them from criminal hacking.
Secure: Penetration testing correctly defined as a specific technique; ethical hacking correctly identified as the broader discipline, with at least one additional technique named.
Developing: Both terms described but the relationship (pen test is a type of ethical hacking) not made clear.

practice_questions.text: Discuss the effectiveness of firewalls and physical security as methods of protecting a network, identifying the limitations of each.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Firewalls — effective at filtering malicious packets from external networks, can block traffic on specific ports and IP ranges, and can alert administrators to suspicious activity. Limitation: firewalls do not protect against threats already inside the network (e.g. an attacker who gains legitimate credentials), and sophisticated attacks may use allowed ports to bypass rules. Physical security — essential because software protections are useless if hardware can be physically removed. Locked server rooms prevent direct tampering; cable management prevents physical interception. Limitation: physical security only protects on-site infrastructure and relies on human behaviour (e.g. not holding doors open for others); it cannot protect data in transit across external networks. Overall: both methods are necessary but neither is sufficient alone — a well-designed network uses multiple overlapping layers of protection.
Secure: Both methods discussed with a valid limitation each; some comparison or evaluative comment.
Developing: Both methods described with one limitation between them; limited evaluation.
Emerging: Only one method discussed meaningfully. [6 marks]
